strengths: The problem has an identifiable audience in high-dimensional classification and factor models. Sparsity of whitened mean contrasts offers an interesting alternative to sparsity of the raw discriminant direction.

The coordinatewise perturbation analysis provides useful technical ideas for controlling estimated whitening transformations. The distinction between whitened and original features is explained clearly in the methodological sections.
The experimental design includes relevant baselines, multiple covariance structures, 200 Monte Carlo replications with reported variability, and two gene-expression applications.
weaknesses: Required correction: the QDA extension is invalid as stated. Equation (5.9) drops coordinates outside the whitened-mean support, although covariance differences can make those coordinates informative. For example, take equal priors, μ1=e1, μ2=2e1, Σ1=I+p uuᵀ, Σ2=I+2p uuᵀ, and u=(0,1,…,1)/√(p−1). These satisfy the relevant sparsity, coherence, and strong-spike conditions. Both whitened means have support {1}, so the proposed population score uses only Z1, while uᵀZ retains additional class information through a variance ratio approaching two. Even with known parameters, the restricted classifier has persistent excess risk. Theorem 6 therefore requires substantive additional assumptions, a different classifier, or removal.

Required theoretical repair: Theorem 3 asserts almost-sure convergence of conditional classification risk under log p=o(n), but Section 8.4 concludes score convergence in probability under the stronger condition (log n)(log p)=o(n). The supplied argument does not establish the stated growth regime or convergence mode. A sharper proof or narrower theorem is necessary. The abstract should also make explicit that Assumption 2 bounds the support size by a constant; a general growing-sparsity result is not established.

Required empirical correction: Table 3 contradicts the specified simulation model. For Model 2, the squared Mahalanobis separation is [10−100ρ/(1+19ρ)]/(1−ρ). At ρ=0.9, the equal-prior Bayes error is approximately 0.0196%, whereas the reported oracle error is 5.40%. This discrepancy cannot reasonably be explained by the reported Monte Carlo variability. Table 1 also repeats several results between ρ=0.7 and 0.8, including an inconsistent oracle value. The simulation implementation, model descriptions, and resulting tables need reconciliation before the performance comparisons provide convincing evidence.

Required qualification: Section 5.1 incorrectly treats Gaussian LDA with its prior-dependent threshold as Bayes optimal for general elliptical distributions. With unequal priors, the likelihood ratio involves log h(q1)−log h(q2), which generally is not the Gaussian linear discriminant. Sub-Gaussian tails do not resolve this issue. Restrict the claim to an appropriate setting, such as equal priors with a common decreasing generator, or analyze the actual Bayes rule.

Required implementation clarification: Section 2.3 defines Λ̂ as the leading eigenvalues of the sample covariance, but subsequently uses D̂=(Λ̂+σ̂²I)^(−1/2), adding the noise variance again. Clarify whether Λ̂ represents total eigenvalues or excess spike strengths, and make the algorithm, derivations, and experimental implementation consistent.

Optional improvements: label model-size comparisons explicitly as counts of transformed or original coordinates. A small number of whitened coordinates can still require all original gene measurements. Sensitivity analyses for the 90% explained-variance rule and departures from exact whitened sparsity would also help readers understand practical applicability.
